- Overestimate prices in early forecast windows, especially after sharp spikes or volatility; reduce initial forecast peaks.
- Underestimate prices in late forecast windows when mean reversion is expected; adjust upward toward historical median or recent trend.
- Overshoot after sudden price spikes; cap forecast peaks at 10–15% below true peak or use moving average smoothing.
- Model tends to overreact to recent volatility; dampen forecast sensitivity to last 5–7 days if volatility > 3%.
- When true outcome is consistently lower than forecast, reduce forecast by 5–10% for next period unless strong fundamentals support higher price.
- If forecast is consistently higher than true outcome, check for lagged data bias — adjust by subtracting 1–2 days of recent high from forecast.
- Avoid overfitting to recent high; use 30-day rolling mean as baseline for correction if forecast deviates > 15% from mean.
- Correct for “forecast drift” — if forecast keeps rising while true price stabilizes or declines, reduce forecast slope by 20–30%.
- When true outcome is below forecast by >10%, assume model is overconfident; apply downward bias of 5–10% for next forecast.
- If forecast is consistently 5–10% above true outcome, reduce forecast by 5–10% for next period unless strong policy or supply shock is evident.
